beats.Meaning: Pre-dawn, Iowa farm near Davenport. Wes follows a low mourning sound into the north field and finds it: a dead Behemoth in the tall grass, one tine snapped. The living machine is prodding it with a manipulator arm, pausing, waiting. Wes stands at the edge of the clearing and watches one Behemoth mourn another.

Pip trots across the clearing without being called and sits down beside the dead machine. The living Behemoth stops prodding. The wail again — quieter. At dawn, the machine begins to move. South. Five miles per hour. Straight line. Pip is male; he has already claimed this as his business.

Wes runs and catches the hull struts while the machine is still building speed. He climbs forty feet to the Crown. Pip appears at the base of the tines below, trotting to keep pace. The Iowa fields begin to roll. He does not stop. Neither does Pip.

CJ Anderson at her outer buffer post in Dixon, Illinois — halfway to Iowa or the edge of the world; didn't matter which. The alert board: unregistered autonomous mass, 5 mph, bearing from Davenport, no transponder, no kill-switch. Hauser wants demolition assets pre-authorized. CJ asks for time. He gives her less than she wants.

First wave of Eigenlift interdiction drones arrives in formation over the Hillsdale cornfields. The machine's scythe-arm takes them down one by one without breaking stride — no urgency, the rotating blade catching each unit clean and dropping it into the corn. Wes watches them fall. Pip does not look up. By the third unit, the formation strategy is visibly futile.

Near Erie. The machine's path crosses a buffer-zone scav camp. Wes shouts from the Crown. A scav attaches a winch line to a forward tine. The machine steps. The tine comes down on the man who was in the way. The threat-wail starts: layered frequencies, electronic shriek on top and something older and wrong underneath. The scavs scatter. The machine keeps walking. It was stepping. It did not deviate.

ArcSec patrol at the scav camp radios CJ: civilian down, machine still mobile, bearing unchanged. Hauser files escalation request four. CJ asks for more time. The old Highway 88 corridor ahead is open farmland — and Eigenlift towers rising out of the corn without transition, thirty stories of GLMZ infrastructure in a flat Iowa-Illinois field.

A larger drone formation arrives near Prophetstown. The machine takes three arm movements to clear them — methodical. After the last unit drops it broadcasts the signal louder, as if answering back. Then the threat-wail fades. The machine resumes its rhythm: five miles per hour, steady footfall, the hull a drum. Wes, awake since before dawn and through the violence, falls asleep on the Crown. When he wakes, the light has changed. He leans over the edge: Pip, still trotting below.

CJ rides out from Dixon on her Eigenlift repulsor skimmer along the 88 corridor — past drone wreckage, past the scav camp aftermath. Near Lyndon she finds Pip: small male terrier, trotting at 5 mph, paws raw, forty miles in like it's just what he does. She scoops him up. He lets her. She calls up to the Crown. A kid answers.

Wes tells CJ about the mourning scene — the dead Behemoth, the living machine prodding it. CJ runs six hours of acoustic telemetry while riding alongside. The broadcast signal is constant: same interval, same rhythm, a question in the pattern. Every matching return reduces the machine's agitation. It came to the largest concentration of humans it could resolve because it believes someone there will answer.

CJ riding alongside on her skimmer, Wes on the Crown — both start transmitting the broadcast pattern back. Wes with his knuckles on the hull, CJ from the ground below. Hauser's fire order goes live. Dixon ahead. The Rock River. The Zone-12 boundary. They are both answering the same question from different directions.

The machine crosses into Dixon. Both Wes and CJ transmit the answer simultaneously. The mourning wail stops. The machine goes still. The new sound arrives — described only by what it is not and what it does to the bodies of the people hearing it. It has no analogue. It is never named.

CJ closes her comms. Hauser's channel goes to static. The machine stands at the edge of Dixon, dormant, framed against an Eigenlift tower and the flat Illinois sky. Nobody fires with a junior ArcSec officer standing ground-side. She does not explain herself. She does not need to.

Wes comes down from the Crown. CJ puts Pip down beside the machine. Pip trots to the nearest tine, sniffs it thoroughly, and lifts his leg. The machine does nothing. The comedy lands right after the sacred moment — the new sound still in everyone's chest, and the dog marking his territory. CJ files her report: behavioral anomaly, origin unknown, threat level zero. She recommends the dead machine in Iowa be left in place. She has never seen it. She does not write the new sound.
